summary: Five short confrontations, back to back. Four men tear open a roof to lower a paralyzed friend to Jesus, and Jesus forgives the man's sins before healing him — which the legal experts hear as blasphemy. He then recruits a tax collector, eats dinner with the wrong crowd, gets questioned about why his followers don't fast, and defends them for picking grain on the Sabbath. By the end of the chapter the opposition is no longer curious. It is building a case.
whyItMatters: Chapter 1 was about authority that amazed people. Chapter 2 is about the same authority starting to offend them. Every scene here asks the same question from a different angle: who does this man think he is, and who gave him permission?

context.author: Anonymous; early tradition names Mark, recording Peter's preaching
context.audience: Non-Jewish readers who need the customs explained — note how the Sabbath dispute is spelled out
context.setting: Capernaum, a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee, and the grain fields around it
context.literaryForm: A cluster of controversy stories — short scenes built around a challenge and a reply, a recognized ancient form

outline.heading: The roof comes off
outline.note: A healing that starts as a forgiveness, and the first charge of blasphemy

outline.heading: Dinner with the wrong people
outline.note: Levi the tax collector is called; the objection is about the guest list

outline.heading: Why don't your people fast?
outline.note: The bridegroom answer, then new cloth and new wine

outline.heading: Grain on the Sabbath
outline.note: David's precedent, and a claim about the Son of Man that goes further than the argument required

keyVerses.text: But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins
keyVerses.why: The healing is offered as evidence for the claim, not the other way round.

keyVerses.text: Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
keyVerses.why: His answer to the guest-list objection, and a statement of who he is actually looking for.

keyVerses.text: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.
keyVerses.why: A principle for reading every rule in the book — the rule exists to serve people, not the reverse.

questions.question: They tore a hole in someone's roof? Is that as destructive as it sounds?
questions.answer: Less than you would think, and still remarkable. A Galilean village house had a flat roof of wooden beams packed with branches and dried mud, reached by an outside stair, used for sleeping and drying grain. You could dig through it and patch it afterward. It was still someone's roof, and four men decided their friend mattered more than the repair bill.

questions.question: The man came for his legs. Why does Jesus start with sins?
questions.answer: Mark doesn't say the paralysis was caused by sin, and it is worth not reading that in. What the sequence does is force the real question into the open. Anyone can say 'your sins are forgiven,' because nobody can check it. So Jesus does the thing that can be checked — the man walks — and offers it as evidence for the claim that cannot be. The healing is the proof, not the point.

questions.question: Why is forgiving sins blasphemy?
questions.answer: Because of who is owed the debt. A person can forgive a wrong done to them; the scribes' objection is that sin is an offense against God, so only God can clear it. Their logic in verse 7 is actually sound. They have correctly identified the size of the claim being made — they simply conclude it must be false.

questions.question: Why is a tax collector such a scandalous person to recruit?
questions.answer: Not because of money handling. Tax collectors in Galilee worked for Herod Antipas and, behind him, Rome — collaborating with the occupying power against their own people — and the system let them keep whatever they squeezed above the quota. The word paired with them, 'sinners,' means people known to be outside the law's requirements. Calling Levi was a public statement about who was welcome, and everyone at that table understood it.

questions.question: Is Jesus saying religious people don't need him?
questions.answer: Verse 17 is edged. Read straight, it says the people who think they are healthy will not send for a doctor — which is a diagnosis of the objectors, not a clean bill of health. He is not conceding that the righteous have no need; he is pointing out that only those who know something is wrong will come.

questions.question: What is fasting, and why would anyone be offended that his followers skipped it?
questions.answer: Fasting means going without food for a set period as an act of grief, repentance, or prayer. Beyond the one day the law required, devout groups fasted regularly by choice, and it marked you as serious. The complaint is that Jesus's group looks casual next to John's disciples and the Pharisees. His answer reframes it: you don't fast at a wedding. The mood fits the occasion, and he is claiming the occasion is a wedding.

questions.question: What do the patch and the wineskins mean?
questions.answer: Both are about a mismatch of materials. New cloth shrinks and rips the old garment it was sewn onto; new wine still fermenting gives off gas, and an old skin that has already stretched and hardened will split. The point is that what Jesus brings cannot be added as a patch to the existing arrangement. It needs its own container. Whether that is a comfort or a warning depends on how attached you are to the old garment.

questions.question: Was picking grain actually illegal?
questions.answer: Taking a handful from someone else's field by hand was explicitly allowed (Deuteronomy 23:25). The objection is not theft, it is timing: plucking heads of grain on the Sabbath could be classified as harvesting, which counted as work. This is a dispute about interpretation, not about a plain command — which is worth knowing, because it means both sides are arguing within the law rather than about whether to keep it.

questions.question: Mark says 'at the time of Abiathar the high priest,' but 1 Samuel 21 says it was Ahimelech. Is that a mistake?
questions.answer: It is a genuine difficulty and readers have handled it several ways. Some take the Greek phrase as 'in the passage about Abiathar,' pointing to the section of scripture rather than the moment. Some note that Abiathar was the far more famous priest of that family and became high priest immediately after, so his name marks the era. Others accept it as a slip. Matthew and Luke both tell the same story without the name, which some read as a quiet correction. It is a small detail and nothing in the argument depends on it.

questions.question: Who is 'the Son of Man'?
questions.answer: It is Jesus's usual way of referring to himself, and it is not modest. In everyday Aramaic the phrase can just mean 'a human being,' but it also reaches back to Daniel 7:13, where 'one like a son of man' comes on the clouds and is given authority over all nations. The phrase lets him make an enormous claim without ever using the word king — useful in a province where claiming kingship got you executed.

glossary.def: Speech that insults God or claims what belongs to God alone. Under the law it was a capital charge, which is why the accusation here is not a small one.

A movement of devout laypeople committed to applying the whole law to daily life, not just temple worship. They were widely respected. In the gospels they are Jesus's most frequent debate partners precisely because they cared enough to argue.
The seventh day, set aside for rest by the fourth commandment. Rest was the command; the disputes were over what counted as work.
Twelve loaves kept in the sanctuary and replaced weekly, which the law reserved for the priests to eat. David's men ate it anyway (1 Samuel 21), which is the precedent Jesus cites.
Jesus's habitual self-title, drawing on Daniel 7:13 where a human figure is given eternal authority by God. It sounds humble and claims a great deal.
